title: Felling the Mind-Tree
summary: The mind is a tree whose branches are the five senses and whose abundant leaves and fruit are hope, and it grows on the water of good and bad. Cut with the axe of the excellent guru's word, Kāṇha says, it does not spring up again; whoever cannot cut it rots, falls and holds to existence, and the last couplet calls for the empty tree to be cut at the root with the axe of the sky. Munidatta reads the refrain as pointing to the tree's non-arising, takes the cutting as cutting its habitual tendencies and making the mind without intrinsic nature, and puts natural clear light where the song has the sky.

lines.gloss: rāga, melody · Mallārī (name of the rāga)

flags.note: The poet's name is not in the heading line itself. It is taken from kāhnupādānāṃ, 'of Kāhnupāda', which the manuscript writes before the song (removed from 1a in the input as not part of the verse), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees: glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody of Kṛṣṇācāryapāda'. It is given in the glossary form Kāṇha; Kāhnupāda or Kāṇhapāda would follow the attribution more closely.

lines.translit: maṇa taru pāñca indi tasu sāhā
lines.gloss: mind · tree · five · senses · its · branches
lines.en: The [mind]{citta} is a [tree]{tree}, the five [senses]{indriya} its [branches]{branch},

flags.note: No verb. The draft takes maṇa and taru as subject and predicate ('the mind is a tree'), as Munidatta does when he says Kṛṣṇācārya imagines his own mind as a tree (cp.45.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) makes maṇa taru one compound, yid ljon, 'mind-tree', and runs the couplet together: yid ljon dbang lnga'i yal ga can de la, 'to that mind-tree with branches of the five senses …'. Either way the mind is the tree; only the syntax differs.

indi = indriya, 'sense faculty' (glossary: senses); tasu, 'its' (Apabhraṃśa genitive), points back to the tree; sāhā = Sanskrit śākhā, 'branch'. Munidatta's lemma spells the first word mana- (cp.45.m2).

lines.translit: āsā bahala pāta phalāhā (ha bāhā) || dhru ||
lines.gloss: hope · abundant, thick · leaves · fruit · (bracketed variant) ha · (bracketed variant) bāhā, 'bears, carries'? · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: Shastri prints (ha bāhā) in brackets after phalāhā, an alternative ending for the line; the pack does not say whether it records the manuscript or his own conjecture. With it the line would end in a verb, bāhā, 'bears, carries' (from vah-): 'hope bears abundant leaves and fruit'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) points that way: 'dod pa 'bab pa'i lo 'bras 'bab par byed, 'makes the leaves and fruit that flow with desire fall (or flow)', ends in a verb ('bab par byed) and seems to take bahala, too, as from vah-, 'flow'. The draft translates the printed text, which has no verb and keeps the parallel with 1a.

Without a verb the relation is open: 'hope [is] its abundant leaves and fruit' (the draft, parallel to 'the five senses its branches'), or 'its leaves and fruit, thick with hope'. bahala (Sanskrit bahula, 'abundant, dense') may qualify the leaves alone or leaves and fruit together. phalāhā is apparently phala, 'fruit', with an ending shaped by the rhyme with sāhā (and bāhā).
Marked with the glossary's {phala}, though that entry describes the 'fruit' of the path; here it is the tree's own fruit. āsā is 'hope' as in the glossary; the Tibetan has 'dod pa, 'desire'.

Shastri prints ধ্রু after this couplet as well as after the refrain and the later couplets. Munidatta names couplet 2 as the refrain (cp.45.m3), so the cue is not translated and does not make couplet 1 the refrain.

lines.gloss: by the excellent guru's word · with the axe · is cut
lines.en: With the [axe]{axe} of the excellent [guru's word]{guru-vacana} it is [cut]{cutting};

flags.note: Two instrumentals stand side by side, baragurubaaṇe, 'by the excellent guru's word', and kuṭhārem̐, 'by the axe': the word is the axe. Munidatta joins them in one compound, varaguruvacanakuṭhāreṇa (cp.45.m3), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) likewise has mchog gi bla ma'i gsung gi sta res bcad, 'cut with the axe of the supreme guru's speech'. chijaa is passive (Sanskrit chidyate); its subject, the tree, is understood from couplet 1 and from 2b.

lines.translit: kāhna bhaṇai taru puṇa na uijaa || dhru ||
lines.gloss: Kāhna · says · tree · again · not · springs up · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: the [tree]{tree} does not spring up again.

flags.note: uijaa is taken as 'springs up, arises' (Sanskrit utpadyate), as Munidatta renders it (punar notpadyate, cp.45.m3); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has slar mi skye, 'does not grow again'. It is kept distinct from bāṭai, 'grows', in 3a. A future sense, 'will not spring up again', is equally possible.

lines.en: That [tree]{tree} grows on the water of [good and bad]{subhasubha};

flags.note: bāṭai is the verb 'grows, increases', not bāṭa, 'road', which it resembles. Munidatta has varddhate, 'grows' (cp.45.m4), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) 'phel, 'increases'.

subhāsubha pāṇī has no case ending; 'on the water' follows the Tibetan chu yis (instrumental) and Munidatta's 'taking the water of its own good and bad, it grows' (cp.45.m4). subhāsubha may mean good and bad deeds or the auspicious and the inauspicious; the Tibetan has dge dang mi dge, 'virtue and non-virtue'.

lines.gloss: cuts · the wise · by the guru's measure · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads mkhas pas dpyod pa bla ma'i tshad kyis ni, 'the learned examine (dpyod pa) by the guru's measure', where the Bengali has chebai, 'cuts'. Its own comment on the couplet has gcod, 'cut' (cp.45.m4), so dpyod may be a slip within the Tibetan or a different reading of the verb. The draft follows the Bengali.

guruparimāṇī: the -ī ending is taken as instrumental, 'by the guru's measure', as in the Tibetan bla ma'i tshad kyis. It could also be a possessive adjective qualifying the wise: 'the wise, who take the guru as their measure'. Munidatta paraphrases: having asked the glorious guru and made his word their own experience (cp.45.m4).
chebai is singular with the collective bidujana, 'the wise'; the object, the tree, is understood from 3a, and 'it' is supplied for English.

lines.translit: jo taru cheba bhebau na jāṇai
lines.gloss: who · tree · cutting · splitting (?) · not · knows
lines.en: Whoever does not know how to [cut]{cutting} and split the [tree]{tree},

flags.note: bhebau is uncertain. It is taken as a second verbal noun beside cheba, 'cutting': 'splitting' (compare Sanskrit bhid-, bheda). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has a pair of cutting words: shing gang gcod dang gtub pa mi shes na, 'if one does not know cutting and chopping the tree'. Munidatta speaks only of cutting (cheda, cp.45.m5). Other analyses (a form of bhāva-, or a final -u meaning 'also') cannot be ruled out.

jo is taken as the relative 'whoever', answered by tā in 4b, like Munidatta's 'those novice yogins who do not know … they' (cp.45.m5). It could also go with taru, 'the tree which …'; the Tibetan shing gang keeps the Bengali order and does not decide it.

lines.translit: saṛi paṛiām̐ re mūṛha tā bhaba māṇai || dhru ||
lines.gloss: having rotted · having fallen · O · fool · he (or: that) · existence · holds to, accepts · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: rotting and falling, you [fool]{mudha}, he holds to [existence]{bhava}.

flags.note: māṇai (Sanskrit mānayati, 'honours, accepts, regards as') is rendered 'holds to'. Alternatives: 'accepts' or 'believes in' existence (the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has srid par mos, 'is devoted to existence'), or, taking tā as 'that', 'takes that for existence'. Munidatta speaks of taking hold of existence again (bhavagraha, cp.45.m5).

saṛi paṛiām̐, 'having rotted, having fallen', are absolutives whose subject is not stated. The draft gives them to the one who cannot cut the tree, as Munidatta (cp.45.m5) and the Tibetan (rul nas ltung) do, but within the image they may belong to the uncut tree. re mūṛha is taken as a vocative, 'you fool'; the Tibetan makes the fool the subject (rmongs nyid).
saṛi is taken as 'rotting' (compare Bengali saṛā, 'rot'); Munidatta's ṣaṭitvā(tvaṃ) seems to render it (cp.45.m5), and the Tibetan has rul, 'rotted'.

lines.en: The empty [tree]{tree}: with the [axe]{axe} of the [sky]{gagana}

flags.note: Shastri prints su[na]taru, restoring na in damaged text. Munidatta's quotation of the line opens suna taruvara (cp.45.m6), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has stong pa'i shing mchog, 'the empty finest tree', where shing mchog is its word for taruvara, 'fine tree', in song 1. Both witnesses therefore read taruvara, and the printed line is two syllables shorter than it would be with vara. The draft translates the song as printed, 'the empty tree', without harmonizing; with the commentary's reading the line would be 'The empty fine tree: with the axe of the sky'.

suna (Sanskrit śūnya) is the adjective 'empty' qualifying the tree, so it is rendered 'empty' and left unmarked rather than forced into the glossary's 'emptiness', a word the sky entry also keeps out of a line that names the sky.

gaaṇakuṭhāra has no case ending, perhaps for the rhyme with ḍāla; 'with the axe of the sky' follows the instrumental of Munidatta's prakṛtiprabhāsvarakuṭhāreṇa (cp.45.m6) and of the Tibetan sta re yis. The Tibetan sets nam mkhar, 'in (or to) the sky', apart as a locative, which could mean the axe is swung in the sky.

lines.translit: chebaha so taru mūla na ḍāla || dhru ||
lines.gloss: cut! (plural) · that · tree · root · not · branch · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: mūla na ḍāla is taken as 'the root, not the branch': cut at the root rather than lop the branches. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports this: shing de'i yal ga rtsa ba nyid nas gcod, 'cut that tree's branches from the very root'. It could also mean 'so that neither root nor branch remains'. Munidatta glosses only the branch: 'by which one is not again subject to the senses' (cp.45.m6).

chebaha is read as an imperative plural, 'cut!'. Munidatta turns it into an address to the novice yogin with a singular imperative, chedaṃ kuru (cp.45.m6); the Tibetan gcod could be imperative or present.

notes.text: [Rāga]{raga}: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song's heading names the one to which it is sung. Mallārī is also the rāga of song 30. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name (mal+lA ri) and calls the piece a glu dbyangs, 'melody'.

The attribution comes from kāhnupādānāṃ, 'of Kāhnupāda', which the manuscript writes before the song; the input removes it from 1a. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song 'the melody called Mallārī, of Nag po spyod pa'i zhabs' (Kṛṣṇācāryapāda), and Munidatta opens by saying that Kṛṣṇācārya, delighted with supreme joy, sets out that same meaning (cp.45.m1).

The image is a tree in full growth, with branches, abundant leaves and fruit, fed by water (3a), and an axe (kuṭhāra, the woodcutter's tool) that fells it so that it does not sprout again (2b). The poem itself names the tree as the mind and its parts as the senses and hope. Cutting at the root, rather than lopping the branches (5b), is what stops a felled tree from growing back.

Munidatta says Kṛṣṇācārya pictures his own mind as a tree, a [poetic fancy]{utpreksa} (utprekṣita), because the mind is the support of the shoots (pallava) of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of beginningless existence; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'branches of tendencies' (bag chags kyi yal ga). He then takes the five senses as its branch (pañcendriyeṇa śākhām adhimucya, 'resolving on the branch as the five senses'), where the Tibetan says the mind-tree is 'freed from (grol ba) the branches of the five senses', as if reading a form of vi-muc; and he repeats hope, leaves and abundant fruit without explaining them (cp.45.m2).

Munidatta's paraphrase of the line, āsā tasya patra(yantra)vahalaphalañ ca, has Shastri's bracketed yantra beside patra, 'leaf', spells bahala as vahala, and has no verb (cp.45.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the comment has 'dod pa de'i lo ma dang 'bras bus 'bab pa, 'desire flows with its leaves and fruit', again taking the word as from vah-, 'flow', as its version of the line does. See the reading flag on (ha bāhā).

Munidatta says the refrain points to the tree's [non-arising]{anutpada}: when its [habitual tendencies]{vasana} are cut with the axe of the excellent guru's word, that mind-tree does not arise again in the ground. He supports this with the Dvikalpa ([Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}): 'the Buddha is not found elsewhere' (na buddho labhyate 'nyatra); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gzhan du sangs rgyas thob mi 'gyur, 'buddhahood is not attained elsewhere' (cp.45.m3).

The poet names himself here, in the refrain ('Kāṇha says'), not in the last couplet. Couplet 5, which the input marks as the bhaṇitā, names no one: it is an exhortation with an imperative (chebaha, 'cut!').

bāṭai, 'grows, increases' (compare Bengali bāṛā, 'increase', and Sanskrit vardhate); Munidatta's varddhate and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) 'phel, 'increases', confirm it (cp.45.m4). The look-alike bāṭa, 'road', is a different word.

Munidatta introduces couplet 3, his second verse, as stating the flow of the guru's word (guruvacanapravāha); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has its 'power' (mthu), as if reading prabhāva. In his paraphrase the mind-tree takes the water of its own good and bad and grows of itself in the ground of beginningless [saṃsāra]{samsara}; then, having asked the glorious guru and made his word their own experience, the wise, whom he glosses as [lords of yogis]{yogindra} (vidujaneti yogīndrāḥ), cut the mind-tree (cp.45.m4). The Tibetan comment reads the middle phrase otherwise: the tree makes 'one's own mind and the rest' circle in the ground of saṃsāra (rang gi yid la sogs pa 'khor ba'i sa gzhir 'khor bar byed), apparently without Shastri's restored [ya] in sva[ya]m.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the line has mkhas pas dpyod pa, 'the learned examine', for chebai bidujana, 'the wise cut'. Its comment calls the wise rig pa dang ldan pa'i skye bo, 'people endowed with knowledge', and has gcod, 'cut' (cp.45.m4), so the verb 'examine' stands only in the Tibetan line.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4, his third verse, as stating the saṃsāric condition of yogins without the teaching lineage (asampradāya; compare [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'yogins without key instruction' (man ngag dang bral ba). The [novice yogins]{balayogin} who do not know the cutting of the mind-tree, which he glosses as making it [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava} (niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa), fall into the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra, take hold of existence again right there (bhavagraha), and do not know the path of liberation (cp.45.m5).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the line, rul nas ltung zhing rmongs nyid srid par mos, 'having rotted, falling, the fool is devoted to existence', takes mūṛha as the subject rather than a vocative and has mos, 'incline to, believe in', for māṇai. Munidatta's ṣaṭitvā(tvaṃ) patanti, 'having rotted (?), they fall', seems to render saṛi paṛiām̐; the Tibetan comment instead has them circle in suffering and fall into the six destinies ('gro ba drug), as if reading ṣaṭ, 'six' (cp.45.m5).

Munidatta introduces the last couplet as praise of the path (mārgānuśaṃsā); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'praise of the path of the guru's word'. He glosses the tree as 'empty of ignorance' (avidyāśūnyataru; the Tibetan comment agrees: ma rig pa stong pa'i shing), addresses the novice yogin, and tells him to cut the habitual tendencies with the axe of natural [clear light]{prabhasvara} (prakṛtiprabhāsvarakuṭhāreṇa), through the guru's lineage. His paraphrase puts clear light where the song has the sky; the Tibetan comment says so outright (nam mkha' zhes te rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba'o: the sky is natural clear light) and has 'by the grace of the guru's word' (bla ma'i gsung gi drin las) for 'through the guru's lineage'. Of the branch he says: by this one is not again subject to the senses (cp.45.m6).

Shastri's printed su[na]taru has na restored in damaged text and no vara. Munidatta's quotation of the line reads suna taruvara (cp.45.m6), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has stong pa'i shing mchog, with shing mchog, 'finest tree', its usual rendering of taruvara (see fine tree). With vara the line gains two syllables. Following the brief, the draft translates the song as it stands, 'the empty tree', and flags the divergence; the reviewer may prefer to emend to suna taruvara, 'the empty fine tree'.

mūla na ḍāla: 'root, not branch'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has shing de'i yal ga rtsa ba nyid nas gcod, 'cut that tree's branches from the very root', which supports cutting at the root. Munidatta cites ḍāla and explains it as that 'by which one does not again come under the power of the senses' (cp.45.m6), recalling 1a, where the senses are the branches.

termsOmitted.reason: Rendered inside the guru-vacana term, 'guru's word', whose listed form is বরগুরুবঅণে; marking guru separately would split that term.
Rendered inside the guru-parimana term, 'guru's measure', whose listed form is গুরুপরিমাণী.

su[na] is the adjective 'empty' qualifying the tree; the entry's English, 'emptiness', would turn the image into a noun of doctrine, and the gagana entry bars 'emptiness' from a line that names the sky. Rendered 'empty', unmarked; see the question on adding 'empty' as a variant.
Detected only in the Tibetan (shing mchog) and in Munidatta's lemma; the draft translates Shastri's printed su[na]taru, which has no vara. See the witness flag and the first question.

questions: 5a: The draft keeps Shastri's su[na]taru, 'the empty tree', because the brief says to translate the song as it stands. Munidatta's quotation of the line (suna taruvara, cp.45.m6) and the Tibetan (stong pa'i shing mchog) both read taruvara, and the printed line is two syllables short of that. Should the line be emended to 'The empty fine tree: with the axe of the sky', with 'fine tree' marked as taruvara, or kept as printed?

1b: Keep the printed phalāhā, which has no verb ('hope its abundant leaves and fruit'), or adopt the bracketed (ha bāhā) as a verb, 'hope bears abundant leaves and fruit', which the Tibetan's closing 'bab par byed seems to reflect? Does Shastri's bracket record the manuscript or his own conjecture?
5a: suna is the adjective 'empty'. The draft leaves it unmarked rather than use 'emptiness'. Should 'empty' be added as a variant of {sunyata} for the adjective?
1b: Is {phala}, whose entry describes the fruit of the path, right for the tree's own fruit here, or should a plain 'fruit' be marked differently, as leaf and branch are?

4b: māṇai is rendered 'holds to' (existence). Would you prefer 'accepts', 'believes in' (the Tibetan has mos), or 'takes that for existence' with tā as 'that'? And should the rotting and falling belong to the fool, as Munidatta (cp.45.m5) and the Tibetan take it, or to the uncut tree?
5b: 'cut that tree at the root, not the branches' (the Tibetan has rtsa ba nyid nas, 'from the very root'), or 'so that neither root nor branch remains'?
3b: 'by the guru's measure' (Tibetan bla ma'i tshad kyis), or 'the wise, who take the guru as their measure'? Also, is the supplied object 'it' acceptable?
4a: bhebau is taken as 'split', beside cheba, 'cut', on the strength of the Tibetan gtub pa, 'chop'. Do you accept that reading?
Song form: the poet's self-naming is in the refrain (2b, 'Kāṇha says'), while couplet 5, which the unit data marks as the bhaṇitā, names no one. Should the unit data be corrected?
Heading: 'Kāṇha' (the glossary form), or 'Kāhnupāda' / 'Kāṇhapāda', following the attribution kāhnupādānāṃ?
